newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to seek to improve inner-city education.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to seek to improve inner-city education.

text.p: In the first of a yearlong series of events to promote racial reconciliation, President Clinton will unveil steps Thursday to improve teaching in poor inner-city and rural areas, a White House official said.

In a speech to the NAACP's annual convention in Pittsburgh, Clinton plans to unveil a proposal to spend $350 million over the next five years to encourage teachers to work in low-income areas and to improve teacher training.

The initiative is Clinton's first effort to reduce the U.S. racial divide since he made a much-publicised speech in San Diego last month warning Americans that the United States risks a return to racial segregation in higher education.
In that speech, Clinton said he planned to lead a one-year effort to promote dialogue on race to try to bring the country together.
At the time, he also named a seven-member panel to examine the state of race relations in the country and give Americans a report outlining problems and possible solutions.
"The president is taking the next step in engaging in this dialogue with some specific policy ideas in the area of education," the White House official, who asked not to be named, said.

While noting that the panel, which began its deliberations with a public meeting Monday, had many different points of view, the official said, "The one thing that they agreed on without any differences is that education is the key."

The official said the $350 million would be spent to offer up to $5,000 a year in scholarships to people studying to be teachers if they agree to work in low-income areas. The money would also be used to give grants to exceptional teacher training institutions to encourage them to expand into low-income areas.

He said the administration hoped the plan would encourage about 35,000 people to teach in needy areas over the five years. The plan, which requires congressional approval, is likely to be included in higher education reauthorization legislation the administration will send Congress later this year, he added.

After addressing the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People's annual convention in Pittsburgh, Clinton was scheduled to speak later in the day to the National Association of Black Journalists in Chicago.

The NAACP is facing an internal debate over integration, which has been the group's goal for more than 80 years. But some in the black community are challenging that policy, saying African Americans need to preserve their own culture.

Asked about the issue Monday, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said, "The president believes that in this increasingly multiethnic, diverse society we live in that learning to live with each other is a source of our future strength."
Another White House official said Clinton was likely to stress this point in his speeches Thursday.
